primary_source_excerpt:
Recent studies have started to explore AI agents for cosmology and scientific discovery 1,2,3,
with early demonstrations on realistic cosmological tasks such as weak-lensing analyses 4. In-
spired by the work on self-evolving agents 5, we discuss two complementary agentic AI systems
that can be applied to scientific discovery in cosmology: one for quantitative tasks with ex-
plicit evaluation metrics, and one for more open-ended scientific workflows. We present our
preliminary results on cosmological applications of our algorithms.
2
Multi-agent systems for scientific discovery
We review the fundamental concepts of AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery. Formally,
an agent A can be modelled as the tuple A = (L, C, τ), where L is the LLM backbone, C is
the context information received, and τ is the tools available for a single agent. Agents solve
problems through multi-agent collaboration. Given a research problem and a dataset D, the
agentic system initiates a high-level goal G, and then follows a policy π to generate a sequence of
actions {a0, . . . , aN} that execute a collection of sub-procedures aimed at advancing the system
towards the solution. The policy may be viewed as a conditional probability distribution over
actions given the high-level goal G, the available tools T , and the context Ct−1 before the decision
step t, such that
at ∼π(· | G, T , Ct−1).
(1)
Autonomous scientific discovery may be formulated as the problem of finding a solution that
maximizes the expected utility of a discovery trajectory. Let
Ξ0:N = (C0, a0, O1, C1, . . . , aN, ON+1, CN+1)
denote the trajectory generated by the agentic system, where Ot represents the observation, tool
output, or experimental result obtained during the discovery process. The system seeks a policy
π∗, such that
π∗= arg maxπ EΞ0:N∼π[U(Ξ0:N; G, D)] .
(2)
Here, U is a task-dependent utility function over the discovery trajectory.
In quantitative
settings, it may be defined by explicit metrics, such as parameter recovery or agreement with
data.
In more open-ended settings, it may instead reflect broader scientific value, such as
generating hypotheses, identifying unexpected patterns, or proposing interpretable explanations.
3
Methodology
We consider the two settings for agentic scientific discovery introduced in Sec. 2: closed tasks
with explicit quantitative objectives, and open-ended scientific workflows with only partially
specified goals.
3.1
CMBEvolve: automated algorithm discovery through LLM-guided tree search
For tasks with explicit quantitative metrics, we use an algorithmic evolution approach to find
the optimal solution. We present CMBEvolve a, a package for automated scientific code evolution
through LLM-guided tree search. Given a task for which the candidate solutions can be evaluated
by a score s, we represent the search process as a rooted tree T = (V, E), where V is the set
of nodes and E the parent-child edges.
Each node belongs to one of the four types: task,
idea generation and selection, code generation, and code mutation. Each node stores search
statistics used by the selection rules, including best score S∗and visit count N, together with
the corresponding generated content and execution outputs. After code evaluation, the score
assigned to a node is backpropagated from that node to the root, updating the statistics of all
ancestor nodes. The general workflow of CMBEvolve is illustrated in Fig. 1(a).
